--- title: Functions error: true --- ## Goals 1. Understand basic syntax of a Julia function. 2. Understand Julia's scoping rules. 3. Develop an awareness of how Julia functions can be used, manipulated, and leveraged. 4. Develop a mental model for writing functions in Julia. ## Overview Functions are the basic units by which we assemble solutions to complex problems. This is especially true in R and Julia, as the languages strongly favor a Functional Programming (FP) style. These languages greatly benefit from ideas in other FP languages (e.g. Lisp) that came before and which evolved concurrently. One key aspect of FP is that functions are treated like any other object in the language (first-class citizens). :::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: callout-note For the Python users, the language favors a particular flavor of object-oriented programming that puts lets emphasis on functions/methods and more on classes. But functions remain important! :::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: ## Syntax and Semantics ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=0} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function func(req1, req2; key1=dflt1, key2=dflt2) # do stuff return out1, out2, out3 end ``` ::: - **Required arguments** are separated by a comma and use *positional notation*. - **Optional arguments** need a default value in the signature. - **Semicolons** are not required in a function call. It is used to separate positional arguments from **keyword arguments**. - A `return` statement is optional, but *highly encouraged in STAT 206*. - If your function needs to return multiple values, use a `Tuple`, `Dict`, or `NamedTuple`. ### Anonymous Functions **Anonymous functions** are functions without a name. - These are short functions in terms of code length. - Used only once and have no reuse value. - Are commonly used in collection functions or list comprehensions. #### Example: Squaring numbers in a collection ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} y = 1:9 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1:9 ``` ::: ::: Use an anonymous function for this straightforward calculation: ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} map(x -> x^2, y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 9-element Vector{Int64}: 1 4 9 16 25 36 49 64 81 ``` ::: ::: Better yet, the `abs2()` function does exactly what we need: ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} map(abs2, y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 9-element Vector{Int64}: 1 4 9 16 25 36 49 64 81 ``` ::: ::: Suppose `abs2()` does not exist. Our function is `^(x, 2)`, it is just the application of the Binary operator `^` with the *second* argument fixed to the value `2`. The `Base.Fix2` construct can help avoid anonymous functions: ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} map(Base.Fix2(^, 2), y) # use sparingly ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 9-element Vector{Int64}: 1 4 9 16 25 36 49 64 81 ``` ::: ::: ### Pass by sharing In Julia, all arguments to functions are **passed by sharing**, in contrast to R and Matlab. ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} x = rand(1:10, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 4-element Vector{Int64}: 9 7 6 6 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} sort!(x) # in-place; vs sort(x) which is out-of-place ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 4-element Vector{Int64}: 6 6 7 9 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 4-element Vector{Int64}: 6 6 7 9 ``` ::: ::: :::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: callout-important Function names ending with `!` indicate that the function mutates at least one argument, typically the first. This is strictly a convention; adding `!` to the end of a Julia function does nothing semantically. :::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: ## Variable scope and rules **Variable scope** and the associated rules defining scope are all about what functions can "see" and "do". - Each function has its own environment, or *local scope*. - Names here override names in the *global scope*. - Internal environment starts with the *named arguments*. - If your computer encounters an undefined name in a function, it looks for it in the environment of the next outer scope *where the function was defined*. This is known as **lexical scope**. Julia, R, and Python all use some variation of these rules for variable scope. That is, they all use *lexical scope* to resolve any "free" variables/symbols. Julia’s scope rules are [more or less straightforward](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/variables-and-scoping/#scope-of-variables). Below are some Julia-specific quirks: - Everything lives in the `Main` module, but default. It is the enclosing global scope for interactive environments; e.g. if you are working in the Julia REPL. - Global references must be declared using `global` for *consistent* behavior. Otherwise, global references will change depending on context, due to [hard vs soft scoping](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/variables-and-scoping/#local-scope). - Julia allows *mutation* of *mutable types*. This reason alone is a good reason to avoid global references at all costs. - Scalars are immutable, as are many other constructs. You cannot change their content. - An `Array` object is mutable, so changing the content of an `Array` instance persists outside a function call. - Remember that `x = ` binds the RHS to the left; `x .= ` fills the LHS with the RHS. :::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: callout-tip ### Avoid global variables! - Reduces risk of confusion and error. - Exception: Reserve global variables for true universal concepts like $\pi$. - Exception: Allocating work buffers in large and sophisticated libraries like BLAS/LAPACK. :::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: ### Example: Using a global variable ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} x = 7 y = ['A', 'C', 'G', 'T', 'U'] function adder(y) global x # specify a global reference x = x + y return x end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` adder (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: Let's see what happens to `x` and `y` when we call the function with a particular value. ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} adder(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} x # oh the humanity! ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5-element Vector{Char}: 'A': ASCII/Unicode U+0041 (category Lu: Letter, uppercase) 'C': ASCII/Unicode U+0043 (category Lu: Letter, uppercase) 'G': ASCII/Unicode U+0047 (category Lu: Letter, uppercase) 'T': ASCII/Unicode U+0054 (category Lu: Letter, uppercase) 'U': ASCII/Unicode U+0055 (category Lu: Letter, uppercase) ``` ::: ::: Outside the `adder()` function: - `x` is a symbol that binds the scalar value `7`. - `y` is a symbol that binds the specified `Array` value. Inside the `adder()` function: - The symbol `y` is declared as a local variable; specifically it is the name of the first (and only) argument to the function. - The symbol `x` is declared as a global reference. We pull its value from the next outer scope. - Surprisingly, we manage to modify `x` but not `y`! ### Example: Redefining `π` In Julia, the symbols `pi` and `π` are defined in the language as convenient references to the number $\pi$. While it is convenient to use, it is a global variable and therefore carries some risk. The following function uses `pi` to compute the area of a circle with radius `r`: ::: {#26 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} circle_area(r) = pi*r^2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` circle_area (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: Check that is works as expected: ::: {#28 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} circle_area.([1, 2, 3]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3-element Vector{Float64}: 3.141592653589793 12.566370614359172 28.274333882308138 ``` ::: ::: What happens if we modify a global constant? ::: {#30 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} truepi = pi pi = 3 circle_area.([1, 2, 3]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3-element Vector{Int64}: 3 12 27 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#32 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} pi = truepi # restore sanity circle_area.([1, 2, 3]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3-element Vector{Float64}: 3.141592653589793 12.566370614359172 28.274333882308138 ``` ::: ::: ## Using functions ### Nesting Functions can be nested. In the example below, the `outerfunction()` can be invoked in the enclosing scope, whereas the `innerfunction()` is only visible within `outerfunction()`. ::: {#34 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function outerfunction() # do some outer stuff function innerfunction() # do inner stuff # can access prior outer definitions end # do more outer stuff end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` outerfunction (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: :::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: callout-tip ### What's the use case? It is sometimes advantageous to hide helper functions where they are used, especially if they are not used elsewhere. Inner functions are also used to create *closures*, functions that "fix" some arguments to another function. We will discuss these at a later date. :::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: ### Recursion Julia supports recursive function definitions. A successful recursive implementation of a function requires two key ingredients: 1. A **base case**. How do we know when to stop recursion? 2. A **recursive step**. How do we build the next item in the recursion? Without a base case, a recursive function will create too many calls to itself and trigger a `StackOverflow` exception. This is a protection built into programming langauges to prevent "runaway code" that never terminates. #### Example: Factorial The following code implements the factorial function, $n! = n \times (n-1) \times \ldots \times 2 \times 1$. ::: {#36 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function myfactorial(n) if n > 1 # recursive step return n * myfactorial(n-1) else # base case; treats x! = 1 for any x <= 0. return 1 end end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` myfactorial (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#38 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @show myfactorial(3) @show myfactorial(6); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` myfactorial(3) = 6 myfactorial(6) = 720 ``` ::: ::: ### Vectorization Scalar functions can be vectorized using the Dot (`.`) syntax: ::: {#40 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # defined for scalar function myfunc(x) return sin(x^2) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` myfunc (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#42 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} x = randn(5, 3) myfunc.(x) # this is applied element-wise; always opt-in ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5×3 Matrix{Float64}: -0.875237 0.132016 0.539914 0.813657 0.0949356 0.000800675 0.961001 0.052414 0.0770759 0.943313 0.752338 0.143938 0.98669 0.976872 0.0624895 ``` ::: ::: Several levels of vectorization can be achieved using `@.`. In particular, this *macro* is a mechanism for *loop fusion*. ::: {#44 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} x = zeros(10) y = randn(10) display(y) @. x = max(0, y) # vectorize `max()` AND `=` ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ``` 10-element Vector{Float64}: -1.421911337494403 -1.6167717418626635 -0.7243949683868441 1.0844290843313644 -0.18635209843632042 1.2256355353834942 -0.7495685831028557 0.7674252451713037 -1.2054847843830778 0.8037208248500304 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 10-element Vector{Float64}: 0.0 0.0 0.0 1.0844290843313644 0.0 1.2256355353834942 0.0 0.7674252451713037 0.0 0.8037208248500304 ``` ::: ::: ### Higher-order functions Julia allows functions as arguments to other functions. You can even write functions to generate other functions. #### `map()` This is a staple of functional languages that allows you to apply a function to each element of a collection: ::: {#46 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} xs = randn(5) map(x -> sin(x^2), xs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5-element Vector{Float64}: -0.298682945514551 0.002138996962536602 0.039566030261310246 0.16661850209842358 0.3475143767326903 ``` ::: ::: The `map()` function and its relatives support `do` block syntax. ::: {#48 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} map(xs) do x sin(x^2) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5-element Vector{Float64}: -0.298682945514551 0.002138996962536602 0.039566030261310246 0.16661850209842358 0.3475143767326903 ``` ::: ::: #### `filter()` Keeps only the elements in a collection for which the predicate function returns `true`. ::: {#50 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} filter(iseven, 1:10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5-element Vector{Int64}: 2 4 6 8 10 ``` ::: ::: #### `reduce()` Combines the elements of a collection from left to right using a binary function to "reduce" it down to a single value. ::: {#52 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} reduce(+, [1, 2, 3, 4]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 10 ``` ::: ::: #### `any()` Tests whether any elements in a collection satisfy the condition defined by a predicate function. ::: {#54 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} any(isodd, 1:10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` true ``` ::: ::: #### `all()` Tests whether all elements in a collection satisfy the condition defined by a predicate function. ::: {#56 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} all(isodd, 1:10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` false ``` ::: ::: #### `count()` Counts how many elements in a collection satisfy the condition defined by a predicate function. ::: {#58 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} count(x -> sqrt(x) < 5, 1:10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 10 ``` ::: ::: #### `sort()` Sorts a collection using a custom metric or transformation defined `by` a function. ::: {#60 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} sort(["apple", "pie", "banana"]; by=length) # sort by string length ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3-element Vector{String}: "pie" "apple" "banana" ``` ::: ::: ### List comprehensions ::: {#62 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} [sin(2i + j) for i in 1:5, j in 1:3] # similar to Python ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5×3 Matrix{Float64}: 0.14112 -0.756802 -0.958924 -0.958924 -0.279415 0.656987 0.656987 0.989358 0.412118 0.412118 -0.544021 -0.99999 -0.99999 -0.536573 0.420167 ``` ::: ::: ## How to write (Julia) functions ### Treat function signatures as interfaces **Interfaces** are the inputs or arguments; the **outputs** or **return value**. - An interface tells the caller what is required. - Outside perspective: Try to avoid caring about *what* is inside a function or *how* it carries out its work. - Calls other functions: `ifelse()`, `abs()`, operators `^` and `>`, and could also call other functions we've written. - Keep the internals orthogonal to the external; that's **encapsulation**. - `return` says what the output is; alternately, return the last evaluation. - We often do not need to care about this; just use `return` to be explicit! - **Comments**: Not required but a good idea. - Helps document what kinds of inputs are required. - Julia and R are dynamic languages. No constructs to enforce types in signatures. - Documentation/comments should signal what is/isn't allowed. ### What should be a function? - Things you're going to re-run, especially if it will be re-run with changes. - Chunks of code you keep highlighting and hitting return on. - Chunks of code which are small parts of a larger analysis or process. - Chunks of code which are very similar to other chunks. ### Named and default arguments Consider the "robust" loss function $$ \psi(x) = \begin{cases} 2 |x| - 1, & x^{2} > 1 \\ x^{2}, & x^{2} \le 1 \end{cases}. $$ We define two versions of this function below: ::: {#64 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # Robust loss function for outlier-resistant regression # Inputs: vector of numbers (x) # Outputs: vector with x^2 for small entries, |x| for large ones function psi1(x) psi = ifelse(x^2 > 1, 2*abs(x) - 1, x^2) return psi end # Robust loss function for outlier-resistant regression # Inputs: vector of numbers (x), scale for crossover (c) # Outputs: vector with x^2 for small entries, 2c|x|-c^2 for large ones function psi2(x; c::Real = 1.0) psi = ifelse(x^2 > c^2, 2*c*abs(x) - c^2, x^2) return psi end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` psi2 (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: Let's check that they are the same when $c=1$: ::: {#66 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} z = 1.3 psi1(z) ≈ psi2(z; c = 1.0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` true ``` ::: ::: Notice that default values are used whenever named arguments are missing: ::: {#68 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} psi2(z; c = 1.0) ≈ psi2(z) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` true ``` ::: ::: Julia enforces order in positional arguments due to its multiple dispatch system. Can't mimic what you see on the R side for shuffling arguments. ### Checking arguments **Problem**: We see odd behavior when arguments are not specified as expected. ::: {#70 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} psi2(z; c = Float64[1, 1, 1, 10]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
TypeError: in keyword argument c, expected Real, got a value of type Vector{Float64}
Stacktrace:

``` ::: ::: ::: **Solution**: Put sanity checks in the code. Ideally, put any input validation at the top of the function body. ::: {#72 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function psi3(x; c::Union{Real,AbstractArray{<:Real}} = 1) if !(c isa Number) error("Parameter `c` should be given as a number. Did you mean `psi3.(x; c = c)`?)") elseif c < 0 error("Parameter `c` should be positive. Got $(c).") end return psi2(x; c = c) # now this is safe! end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` psi3 (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#74 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} psi3(z; c = Float64[1, 1, 1, 10]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ### Encapsulation: Respect the interfaces! - Interfaces mark out a controlled environment for our code. - A function interacts with the rest of a system *only at the interface*. - Similarly, the "output" should only be through the return value. - That means avoiding *side-effects*, which are modifications to some external state not defined inside a function. Your goal in writing a function is to achieve **encapsulation**: separate *what* your function does from *how* it implements its task. - It should do one and only one thing as well as possible. - If your function needs to modify some state/data, then that state/data ought to be arguments to the function. - Information that is unrelated to what a function does should be minimized as much as possible.
